Investigating Plant-based vs. Meat-based Diets for Dogs

Author

Anna Ly

Published

October 1, 2024

Dataset Sourcing & Application

We are using the “Vegan versus meat-based pet foods” dataset found on https://osf.io/nbepu/. A survey, approved by the UK General Data Protection Regulation, was deployed online and advertised through social media platforms and advertisements for dog owners from May 2020 to December 2020. More details can be found in [1].

The aim is to predict a dog’s diet type, meat-centric or plant-centric, based on health issues and demographic factors. Society believes it is animal abuse to feed a dog a plant-based diet since their ancestor, wolves, are carnivores; this analysis will help assess the association between a dog’s health and their diet.

In the survey, participants specified their dog’s diet, including raw, kibble, home-cooked, pescetarian, vegetarian, and vegan. Vegetarian and vegan diets were categorized as “plant-centric” and the others as “meat-centric.” Although the questionnaire allowed for other diet types, such as insects, only 26 responses included this, so they were excluded from the analysis.

Data Transformation & Exploratory Data Analysis

After removing columns containing short answer responses, as well as users who answered “unsure” to at least one of the closed-form questions, 297 responses were removed (the amount of rows of missing values), which led to a total of (n = 2342) participants. 183 of 297 were removed since most participants did not want to admit to their household income.

The analysis uses 13 variables in total, with an extra 2 due to one-hot encoding (the owner’s gender and dog’s sex were each split into male/female indicators). Here is a brief summary of the data types for the selected variables:

  • Numeric (transformed by the average of the range): owner’s age, dog’s age.

  • Ordinal categorical (transformed into numeric): education level, household income, breed size, number of vet visits, dog’s health, owner’s meat consumption.

  • Categorical (some transformed into binary): owner’s gender, dog’s sex, dog’s neuter status, whether the dog is on prescription medication, dog diet.

Furthermore, many questions asked for a range instead of a numerical value (such as age), so responses were transformed by taking the midpoint of the provided range. The exact details, including data cleaning, are shown in the supplementary material section.

Since most of the data came from closed-form questions which involved ranges, there were no extreme outliers. Surprisingly, there are outliers for highly educated dog owners who feed their dogs a meat-based diet (see Figure 2 in the supplementary material).

Due to space limitations, not all variables are discussed, but summary tables for income level and gender of the participants are provided:

More summary tables (3–9) are included in the supplementary material. Associations are also observed between a dog’s diet and both the owner’s diet and the dog’s overall health:

The data were split into a training set (n = 781, 33.34%), a validation set (n = 781, 33.34%) and a hold-out set (n = 780, 33.33%) since the dataset is large and equal proportions allowed the models to be trained, validated, and tested fairly.

K-Nearest Neighbour Analysis

  1. No further transformations beyond those described above were necessary.

  2. Values from \(K = 1, \ldots, 5\) were tested to compute the misclassification error on the validation set. A value of \(K = 5\) gave the lowest error rate.

  3. For K-nn, the most important predictor cannot be determined in a straightforward manner: one would need to iteratively remove a variable one at a time to see if this drastically changes the accuracy.

Model Evaluation: the K-nn algorithm predicts the hold-out set with a 86.41% accuracy, so the misclassification rate is 13.59%.

Logistic Regression Analysis (Without Shrinkage)

  1. The dog’s diet variable was transformed to binary: meat-centric is 1, plant-centric is 0.

  2. The ROC curve was used to help determine a cut-off value. An initial cut-off of 0.5 was tried, but the ROC curve suggested a cut-off of approximately 0.73.

  3. The most important predictors in classifying the response are the owner’s diet and the owner’s gender. In particular, owners who consume less meat and are female are more likely to give their dog a plant-based diet.

  4. For a one-unit increase in the owner’s diet (where the ordered categories are omnivore, flexitarian, pescetarian, vegetarian, and vegan), the odds of an owner feeding their dog a meat-based diet decrease by approximately 0.25. Similarly, the odds of men feeding their dog a meat-based diet decrease by approximately 0.29.

Model Evaluation: The misclassification rate for the logistic regression model without penalty for the hold-out set is 87.05%, which means the model is accurate 12.95% of the time.

Compared to the K-nn algorithm, the logistic regression model (without shrinkage) is significantly worse at predicting the dog’s diet.

Logistic Regression (With Shrinkage)

  1. The shrinkage value that performs best on this data set is \(\lambda = 0.01253655\).

  2. The model with shrinkage eliminates most of the covariates. The remaining covariates are: education level, owner’s age, owner’s diet, dog’s age, and number of vet visits.

  3. The misclassification error rate for the logistic regression model with shrinkage for the hold-out set is 88.84%. This is worse than the model without shrinkage. This could be caused by the fact that logistic regression may be a poor way to model the data (i.e., there are model assumptions) or that transformations of the covariates are required to properly fit the dataset.

Conclusions from Analysis

The K-nn algorithm outperforms logistic regression (both with and without shrinkage) in predicting a dog’s diet. Both logistic regression models show that owner’s diet is strongly associated with the dog’s diet. The relationship between the owner’s diet and the dog’s diet is intuitive; owners who eat less meat are likely to feed their pets less meat.

Fortunately, dogs with a plant-based diet do not seem to have more health complications compared to their meat-eating counterparts, but this could be due to participation bias: owners who feed their dogs a plant-based diet may insist their dogs are healthy to justify their peculiar diet.

Is Generative AI Possible?

If you use Bing Copilot, you could try asking it to find a dataset; however, none of the ones it suggested were usable for this project. If provided a link to a dataset, Bing Copilot would create a description that sounds legitimate but it would not accurately capture how the dataset was properly sourced.

Furthermore, if asked to do some exploratory data analysis, it would suggest code that was not ready to use. However, with enough prompting and context from the user, it provided practical code for data cleaning, printing out summaries, potential graphs, model building, and some analysis.

Hence, it can do large portions of the assignment but would struggle in the beginning with picking a viable dataset and properly citing the source material. Prompts are shown in [2], [3], [4], and [5].

data_transformation_ref.R

This code was used as a reference for how the survey responses were transformed into binary or quantitative variables.

Code 
# Github Copilot helped write some of these.
dog_diet_levels = c("Meat-based – conventional"   = "Meat", "Meat-based – raw" = "Meat",
  "Meat-based – lab-grown"  = "Meat", "Vegan (consuming no animal products)" = "Plant",  "Vegetarian (including eggs or milk, but not meat)" = "Plant", "Mixture" = "Other",
  "Fungi-based" = "Other", "Insect-based" = "Other", "Algae–based" = "Other", "Unsure" = "Other")

owner_diet_levels = c("Omnivore (i.e. eat meat)" = 0, "Omnivore reducing animal product consumption" = 1, "Pescatarian (including fish but no other meats)" = 2, "Vegetarian (consuming plants, eggs and milk)" = 3, "Vegan (consuming no animal products)" = 4)

education_levels = c("Did not complete high school" = 0, "High school or equivalent" = 1, "College or University award lower than undergraduate degree" = 2, "University undergraduate degree" = 3, "University postgraduate degree lower than doctoral degree e.g. masters" = 4, "Doctoral degree" = 6)

income_levels = c("Low" = 0, "Medium" = 1, "High" = 2)

health_levels = c("Seriously ill" = 0, "Significant or frequent problems" = 1, "Generally healthy with minor or infrequent problems" = 2, "Healthy" = 3)

age_ranges = c("18-19" = 18.5, "20–29" = 24.5, "30–39" = 34.5, "40–49" = 44.5, "50–59" = 54.5, "60–69" = 64.5, ">70" = 80)

dog_sizes = c("Toy (≤ 4.1 kg or ≤ 9 lb)" = 0, "Small (4.5–10.9 kg or 10–24 lb)" = 1, "Medium (11.4–22.3 kg or 25–49 lb)" = 2, "Large (22.7–40.5 kg or 50–89 lb)" = 3, "Giant (> 40.9 kg or > 90 lb)" = 4)

vet_visit_range = c("0" = 0, "1" = 1, "2" = 2, "3" = 3, ">3" = 4)

binary_yn = c("Yes" = 1, "No" = 0)

neuter_statuses = c("sexually intact" = 0, "castrated" = 1, "spayed" = 1)

main_work.R

These were the initial data cleaning steps. The analysis uses the libraries created by [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], and [12] in the order of the loaded libraries.

Code 
library("tidyverse"); library("readxl"); library("class"); library("ROCR")
library("pROC"); library("glmnet")

source("data_transformation_ref.R")

my_data = read_excel("Canine health results.xlsx", sheet = 2)

# Columns removed due to missing data / long-answer format
remove = c(seq(1, 6, by = 1), 8, 13, 14, 17, 19,  seq(21, 32, by = 1),
           seq(36, 45, by = 1), seq(46, 58, by = 1))

my_data = my_data[, -remove]

my_data = na.omit(my_data)

names(my_data) = c("education_lvl", "household_income", "owner_age", "owner_gender",
                   "owner_diet", "breed_size", "dog_age", "sex_and_neuter_status",
                   "vet_visit", "dog_meds", "dog_health", "dog_diet")

my_data = my_data %>%
  separate("sex_and_neuter_status", into = c("dog_sex", "neuter_status"), sep = ", ")

# Github Copilot helped write some of these data cleaning steps.
my_data = my_data[my_data$household_income != "Prefer not to answer", ]
my_data = my_data[my_data$owner_gender != "Prefer not to answer", ]
my_data = my_data[my_data$owner_diet != "Other", ]
my_data = my_data[my_data$dog_age != "Unsure", ]
my_data = my_data[my_data$vet_visit != "Unsure", ]
my_data = my_data[my_data$dog_health != "Unsure", ]
my_data = my_data[my_data$owner_gender != "Other", ] # Only 4 people identified as "other"

pre_cleaning_dat = my_data

# Github Copilot helped write some of these data mutation steps.
my_data = my_data %>%
  mutate(education_lvl = education_levels[education_lvl]) %>%
  mutate(household_income = income_levels[household_income]) %>%
  mutate(owner_age = age_ranges[owner_age]) %>%
  mutate(neuter_status = neuter_statuses[neuter_status]) %>%
  mutate(owner_diet = owner_diet_levels[owner_diet]) %>%
  mutate(breed_size = dog_sizes[breed_size]) %>%
  mutate(dog_age = as.numeric(dog_age)) %>%
  mutate(vet_visit = vet_visit_range[vet_visit]) %>%
  mutate(dog_meds = binary_yn[dog_meds]) %>%
  mutate(dog_health = health_levels[dog_health]) %>%
  mutate(dog_diet = dog_diet_levels[dog_diet]) %>%
  mutate(
    owner_male = if_else(owner_gender == "Male", 1, 0),
    owner_female = if_else(owner_gender == "Female", 1, 0),
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    dog_male = if_else(dog_sex == "Male", 1, 0),
    dog_female = if_else(dog_sex == "Female", 1, 0),
  )

my_data = my_data %>%
  select(-owner_gender, -dog_sex)

my_data = my_data[my_data$dog_diet != "Other", ]

K-nn algorithm:

Code 
set.seed(1)
full_set = 1:2342
train_sample = sample(full_set, 781, replace = FALSE)
valid_sample = sample(setdiff(full_set, train_sample), 781, replace = FALSE)
test_sample = setdiff(full_set, c(train_sample, valid_sample))

covariates = dplyr::select(my_data, -dog_diet)
response = as.factor(pull(my_data, dog_diet))

data_train = slice(my_data, train_sample)
data_valid = slice(my_data, valid_sample)
data_test = slice(my_data, test_sample)

data_x_train = dplyr::select(data_train, -dog_diet)
data_y_train = dplyr::pull(data_train, dog_diet)
data_x_valid = dplyr::select(data_valid, -dog_diet)
data_y_valid = dplyr::pull(data_valid, dog_diet)
data_x_test = dplyr::select(data_test, -dog_diet)
data_y_test = dplyr::pull(data_test, dog_diet)

K = as.list(c(seq(1,10, by = 1)))

Compute_KNN_test_error = function(k){
  knn_pred_test = knn(data_x_train, data_x_valid,data_y_train, k = k)
  return(1-mean(knn_pred_test == data_y_valid))
}

test_erro_k = lapply(K, Compute_KNN_test_error)

ggplot(
  tibble(K = unlist(K), test_error = unlist(test_erro_k))) +
  geom_point(aes(x = K, y = test_error)) +
  geom_line(aes(x = K, y = test_error)) +
  ylab("Test error")
Code 
knn_pred_1 = knn(train = data_x_train, test = data_x_test, cl = data_y_train, k = 9)

mean(knn_pred_1 == data_y_test)

Logistic regression (without shrinkage):

Code 
my_data_binary = my_data %>%
  mutate(dog_diet = if_else(dog_diet == "Meat", 1, 0))

glm.fit = glm(dog_diet ~ education_lvl + household_income + owner_age + owner_diet + breed_size + dog_age + neuter_status + vet_visit + dog_meds + dog_health + owner_male + dog_male, data = my_data_binary, family = binomial("logit"), subset = train_sample)

pred_prob = predict(glm.fit, newdata = slice(my_data, valid_sample), type = "response")

pred_df = tibble(pre_prob = pred_prob,
  Y = slice(my_data, valid_sample) %>% pull(dog_diet))

cutoff = 0.5
pred_df = dplyr::mutate(pred_df, dog_diet_predicted = ifelse(pre_prob > cutoff, 1, 0))

tab = table(pred_df$Y, pred_df$dog_diet_predicted)

pred = prediction(pred_df$pre_prob, pred_df$Y)

pROC_graph = roc(pred_df$Y, pred_df$pre_prob, smoothed = TRUE, ci = TRUE, ci.alpha = 0.9, plot = TRUE, auc.polygon = TRUE, max.auc.polygon = TRUE, grid = TRUE, print.auc = TRUE, show.thres = TRUE)

Code 
test_set_pred_log_odds = predict(cv_lasso, newx = X[test_sample, ], s = "lambda.1se")[,1]

test_set_pred_prob = exp(test_set_pred_log_odds)/(1 + exp(test_set_pred_log_odds))

df_lasso_test = tibble(pre_prob = test_set_pred_prob,
  y = slice(my_data_binary, test_sample) %>% pull(dog_diet))

cutoff = 0.6944256

dog_diet_test_lasso = dplyr::mutate(
  df_lasso_test,
  dog_diet_predicted = ifelse(
    pre_prob <= cutoff,
    my_data_binary$dog_diet[1],
    my_data_binary$dog_diet[2]
  )
)

tab = table(pull(df_lasso_test, y), pull(dog_diet_test_lasso, dog_diet_predicted))

1- sum(diag(tab))/sum(tab) # miss-classification error rate
